title: Web Crawler
brief: Design a crawler that starts from a few seed addresses, downloads pages, finds the links in them and follows those links, until it has collected a large slice of the web. The hard parts are not the download. They are being polite to every site and never fetching the same thing twice.

functional: Start from a list of seed URLs and follow links found in pages.
Download each page and store the raw content for later processing.
Obey robots.txt, the file where a site says what may be fetched.
Never download the same URL, or the same content, twice.
Come back to pages later, more often when they change often.
Stay inside limits so a site that makes endless links cannot trap it.

nonFunctional.name: Politeness
nonFunctional.target: At most one request at a time to a host, with a delay between requests

nonFunctional.name: Throughput
nonFunctional.target: Finish a first pass of the target set inside the crawl window

nonFunctional.name: Robustness
nonFunctional.target: Bad HTML, slow servers and dead links never stall the crawl

nonFunctional.name: Extensibility
nonFunctional.target: New content types or processing steps plug in after the fetch

estimate.note: All numbers are assumptions you can change. Two things shape the design: how fast pages must be fetched to fit the window, and how much memory it takes to remember every URL already seen.

evolution.title: One loop
evolution.problem: Start with the simplest thing that works: a queue of URLs and one worker.
evolution.change: Take a URL, download it, save it, pull out the links and push them back on the queue.

evolution.title: Politeness: a queue per host
evolution.problem: Many workers pop URLs from one queue and a thousand of them land on the same site at once. The site slows down or bans us.
evolution.change: Split the frontier into two layers. A front layer ranks URLs by value. A back layer keeps one queue per host. A host is released to one worker at a time, then rests for a delay.
evolution.numbers: hosts active at once = pages per second times the delay

evolution.title: DNS and robots.txt caches
evolution.problem: Every fetch first needs the host's address and its robots.txt rules. Looking both up each time doubles the work and DNS becomes the slowest step.
evolution.change: Cache DNS answers and each host's parsed robots.txt with an expiry. A URL that is not allowed is dropped before any request is sent.

evolution.title: Never queue a URL twice
evolution.problem: Pages link to each other, so the same URL arrives thousands of times. The frontier grows without end and the crawl loops forever. A calendar page can generate links without limit.
evolution.change: Normalise each URL, check a depth and length limit, then ask a seen set. Only new URLs enter the frontier. The seen set is a Bloom filter in memory in front of a sharded key-value store.
evolution.numbers: the estimator compares exact hashes with a Bloom filter

evolution.title: Same page, different URL
evolution.problem: Mirrors, tracking parameters and printer-friendly copies are one page under many URLs. The seen set cannot catch them, so storage and later processing double up.
evolution.change: Hash the page body, or a fingerprint that tolerates small changes. If the hash is already known, skip storing and skip following its links again.

evolution.title: Priority and recrawl
evolution.problem: A news front page changes hourly and a dead blog never does. A first-in first-out frontier wastes the window on both.
evolution.change: A scheduler estimates each page's change rate from past fetches and puts it back into the frontier when it is due. The front layer ranks by page value and how stale it is.

steps.say: The front layer of the frontier picks a valuable, due URL and routes it to its host's queue.
A free worker asks for work. The host queue releases a URL only if that host has rested for its delay.
The worker checks the cached robots.txt rules for the host. If the path is disallowed, it stops here.
It resolves the host name from the DNS cache and falls back to a real lookup only on a miss.
It downloads the page, with a timeout and a size cap so a slow or huge reply cannot stall it.
It hashes the body and asks the content store if this page was seen under another URL.
A new page goes into the raw page store. A duplicate is dropped.
The worker passes the downloaded page to the parser.
The parser extracts every link, and turns relative ones into full URLs.
Dedupe normalises each URL: lowercase host, drop fragments and tracking parameters, sort query keys. It rejects ones past the depth and length limits.
It asks the seen set. The Bloom filter answers from memory, and a maybe is confirmed in the key-value store.
Only new URLs go to the frontier, with a priority guessed from the source page and depth.
The scheduler compares each page's change rate with its age and finds those that are due.
It puts them back in the frontier. Pages that change often come back sooner.
The fetch sends the stored ETag. A not-modified reply costs almost nothing and tells the scheduler to wait longer next time.

deepDives.title: Remembering every URL
deepDives.question: How do we know a URL was seen, when there are billions of them?

options.name: Exact set in a database
options.pros: No mistakes. Easy to reason about.
options.cons: Billions of random lookups. Big, and the slowest part of the loop.

options.name: Bloom filter only
options.pros: A few bits per URL, held in memory, answers in microseconds.
options.cons: Some new URLs are wrongly skipped. It cannot delete, and it must be rebuilt as it fills.

options.name: Bloom filter in front of a sharded store
options.pros: Most 'seen' answers come from memory. Only the maybes reach the store.
options.cons: Two layers to run. The filter and store can drift apart.

deepDives.pick: Bloom filter in front of a sharded store
deepDives.because: A wrong skip costs one missed page, and a wrong include costs one duplicate fetch. Use the filter to answer 'definitely new' fast, and the store to settle the rest. Shard by URL hash.

deepDives.title: Shape of the frontier
deepDives.question: How do we pick the next URL and still be polite?

options.name: One FIFO queue
options.cons: No priorities, and a burst of one site's links hits it all at once.

options.name: Priority queues only
options.pros: Valuable and stale pages go first.
options.cons: Nothing stops many workers hammering one host.

options.name: Priority layer, then per-host queues
options.pros: Front layer decides value. Back layer decides who is allowed now. Each concern is separate.
options.cons: More moving parts. Needs a map from host to worker so one host's queue has a single reader.

deepDives.because: Politeness is a hard rule and priority is a preference, so they are different layers. Assign each host to one worker with consistent hashing, so its delay is kept without any lock.

deepDives.title: Same content, many URLs
deepDives.question: How do we avoid storing and following near-identical pages?

options.name: Exact content hash
options.pros: Cheap and exact. Catches mirrors and tracking-parameter copies.
options.cons: One changed byte, such as a timestamp, makes a new hash.

options.name: Similarity fingerprint (SimHash)
options.pros: Near-copies get near fingerprints, so small edits still match.
options.cons: Needs a nearness lookup, and the threshold needs tuning.

deepDives.pick: Exact hash first, fingerprint for near copies
deepDives.because: The exact hash is nearly free and catches most copies. Run the heavier fingerprint only on pages that pass it, to catch pages that differ by a banner or a date.

deepDives.title: Escaping spider traps
deepDives.question: A page produces endless new URLs, such as a calendar with a next-month link forever. What stops the crawler?

options.name: Depth and URL length limits
options.pros: Simple and effective. Cuts most loops.

options.name: Per-host page budget
options.pros: Bounds the damage from any one site.
options.cons: A genuinely huge site gets under-crawled.

options.name: Detect repeating patterns
options.pros: Finds traps early, such as the same path pattern many times.
options.cons: Heuristic, and false alarms drop real pages.

deepDives.pick: Depth, length and per-host budgets together
deepDives.because: No single rule is perfect, so stack cheap limits. Raise a host's budget if its pages are valuable, and let a human whitelist the huge sites.

failures.what: A site is slow or hangs
failures.impact: Workers wait on it and the whole crawl slows down.
failures.fix: Timeouts and size caps on every request. Back the host off exponentially after errors, and let its queue sleep.

failures.what: A spider trap or a link farm
failures.impact: The frontier fills with endless useless URLs from one host.
failures.fix: Depth, URL length and per-host budgets. Alert when one host's share of the frontier jumps.

failures.what: A worker crashes holding a URL
failures.impact: That URL is lost, and its host's queue may be stuck as in flight.
failures.fix: Give each handed-out URL a lease. If it is not marked done before the lease ends, the URL goes back to its queue. Fetching is safe to repeat.

failures.impact: Every known URL looks new, and the crawler refetches the web.
failures.fix: Keep the sharded store as the source of truth and rebuild the filter from it. Content hashes still stop duplicate storage.

failures.impact: Complaints and IP bans, which block every later fetch.
failures.fix: One reader per host queue, a honoured crawl delay, and a global per-host cap. Identify the crawler in its user agent with a contact address.

scaling.limit: One frontier cannot hold the whole web
scaling.lever: Shard the frontier by host with consistent hashing. A host then lives on exactly one node, which keeps politeness local.

scaling.limit: Seen set memory grows with every URL
scaling.lever: Shard the filter by URL hash. Use a counting or layered filter, and rebuild it from the store on a schedule.
Run crawler clusters in several regions, each owning hosts near it. Compress pages before storing them.

recap.key: Fetching is easy. Politeness (a queue per host with a delay) and never repeating work (URL seen set, content hash, trap limits) are the design.
recap.numbers: 1B pages in 7 days is about 1,650 pages per second and 1.3 Gbit/s. The seen set is 1.25 GB as a Bloom filter at 10 bits per URL.
moves: Two-layer frontier: priority first, then a queue per host
Cache DNS and robots.txt, and check before fetching
Normalise URLs, then Bloom filter plus sharded store
Hash content to skip copies, and schedule recrawls by change rate
